# An attained-counterexample reduction for the stronger finite-base target

UPDATE 2026-09-18: the numerical target for arbitrary finite bases is
FALSE; see `candidate 640d07cd1de2a423`.
The conditional compactness theorem below is not refuted by that example,
but no universal numerical closure in its unrestricted class is possible.
For original lattice bases, retain the extra completeness property proved
in `candidate 2086e4eaa4bce465`.

This is an auxiliary compactness theorem. It neither proves the
finite-base target below nor proves Oertel's conjecture. It allows a
strict counterexample on one fixed finite base to be replaced by an
attained, all-positive counterexample on a canonical lifted minor of
that base.

## 1. Definitions and the target under discussion

Fix d≥1. For a nonempty finite set P in a Euclidean space, an actual
positive fiber family is a collection of d-dimensional compact convex
bodies K_p⊂R^d, p∈P, satisfying

    Σ_p λ_p K_p ⊂ K_q whenever q=Σ_p λ_p p,
    λ_p≥0, Σ_p λ_p=1, q∈P.                              (1)

Equivalently, the convex hull of the fibers has exactly K_q as its
section at every specified q∈P. Only these specified fibers are
measured. Their measure is Σ_p vol_d, and their candidate centers are
the points of their union S_P. Let

    D_P(K)=max_{y∈S_P} inf_{closed H∋y} μ(S_P∩H)/μ(S_P),
    b_d(P)=inf_K D_P(K).                                (2)

Halfspaces belong to aff(P)×R^d; using a larger Euclidean ambient
space gives the same definition. A containing halfspace that contains
the whole affine hull contributes full measure and cannot lower depth.
The maximum in (2) exists: depth is uniformly Lipschitz within each
bounded fiber, as proved below, and there are finitely many compact
candidate fibers.

Write h(P) for the least positive integer h with the following
property: whenever a finite family of ambient convex sets has common
intersection disjoint from P, some subfamily of at most h members also
has common intersection disjoint from P. This number exists and is at
most |P|, by choosing one excluding member per point. The
stronger finite-base target considered here is

    b_d(P) ≥ γ_d/h(P),   γ_d=(d/(d+1))^d.                (3)

No claim of (3) is assumed in this note.

The ordinary continuous Grünbaum theorem does give the elementary
bound b_d(P)≥γ_d/|P|>0: choose a fiber of at least the average mass
and its centroid; every containing ambient halfspace receives the
stated proportion from that fiber alone. Consequently every attained
minimum below has strictly positive depth, and a bad minor must have
|U|>h(U).

A set U⊂P is closed if U=P∩conv(U). Let L(U) consist of the scalar
functions on U preserving every anchored convex representation.
Choose a basis 1,g_1,...,g_{ℓ-1} of L(U), and denote by Φ(U) the finite
set of vectors (g_1(u),...,g_{ℓ-1}(u)), u∈U. Different bases produce
affinely equivalent sets and do not change (2). Thus Φ(U) is a
canonical base up to harmless affine equivalence.

## 2. The finite collection of canonical minors

Consider the finite collection

    {Φ(U): ∅≠U⊂P, U=P∩conv(U)}.                         (4)

The lift preserves every anchored convex representation, in both
directions. The forward implication follows from the definition of
L(U); the reverse implication follows by projecting to the original
coordinates, which are affine functions of Φ(u). Consequently it
preserves closed traces, dependence components, and h(U). Also

    L(Φ(U))=Aff(Φ(U)).                                   (5)

These statements and their proofs are given in Sections 1, 2, and 4 of
`candidate dbf3b23d25004153`.

The collection (4) is closed under the minor operation needed below.
Indeed, a closed subset of Φ(U) corresponds to a closed subset T of U.
Because U is P-closed, T is P-closed too:
P∩conv(T)⊂P∩conv(U)=U, and its intersection with U is T. Anchored
representations on the restricted Φ(U)-base correspond exactly to
those on T. Taking its universal lift therefore gives a base affinely
equivalent to Φ(T), already in (4). The same applies to dependence
components, which are closed subsets.

For later use, h(T)≤h(U) when T is U-closed. Every T-closed trace is
then U-closed, and any minimal infeasible trace family on T is also a
minimal infeasible trace family on U, with the same witness points.

## 3. Lifting and discarding mass

If the same compatible fibers are placed at Φ(U) instead of at U,
the affine projection (Φ(u),x)↦(u,x) preserves the measure and sends
the lifted union onto the original union. Every original containing
halfspace pulls back to a lifted containing halfspace. Therefore

    D_{Φ(U)}(K) ≤ D_U(K).                                (6)

This is a statement about full residual fibers, with every oblique and
closed halfspace included. There is no replacement by weighted atoms.

If T⊂U and M_T is the mass of its retained fibers, then for every
candidate in those fibers, every containing halfspace has at least
its retained mass. Taking infima and maxima gives

    D_U(K) ≥ (M_T/M_U) D_{T in U}(K).                    (7)

Here the right-hand depth is calculated on the restricted fibers in
their inherited affine base. Applying their canonical lift can only
decrease that depth, by (6).

## 4. Existence of a minimal bad canonical minor

Assume there exists an actual positive family on P with

    D_P(K)<γ_d/h(P).                                    (8)

Equation (6) makes Φ(P) a bad member of (4), meaning
b_d(Φ(P))<γ_d/h(P). Choose among all bad members Φ(U) one with the
smallest number |U| of base points. Put

    B=Φ(U),  h=h(U),  β=b_d(B)<γ_d/h.                    (9)

This selection is over a nonempty finite collection. It requires no
existence of a minimizing family yet.

The base U, and hence B, is dependence-connected. Otherwise write its
components as U_i and h_i=h(U_i). Exact Helly additivity gives
Σ_i h_i=h. For any bad family on B of total mass M, one component has

    M_i/h_i ≥ M/h.

By (7), its restricted depth is at most D_B M/M_i, strictly less than
γ_d/h_i. Lift that restricted family to Φ(U_i). Equation (6) preserves
the strict inequality. Since U_i is a proper closed subset of U, this
contradicts the minimality of |U|. This proves connectedness.

## 5. A minimizing sequence cannot lose positive fibers

Take a sequence of positive actual families on B with total mass one
and D_B(K_j)→β. Scaling all continuous coordinates makes this
normalization without changing depth or compatibility. Along a
subsequence every normalized fiber mass converges, say to w_u≥0,
with Σ_u w_u=1. Let T={u:w_u>0}.

The set T is U-closed. If z is a convex combination of points of T,
choose one source u with coefficient λ>0. Fix points in the other
source fibers in (1); the target contains a translate of λK_{j,u}.
Thus |K_{j,z}|≥λ^d|K_{j,u}|, whence w_z≥λ^d w_u>0.

Suppose T is proper. Its retained total mass tends to one. Equations
(7) and (6) imply

    b_d(Φ(T)) ≤ liminf_j D_{T in B}(K_j) ≤ β.

To justify the second inequality explicitly, (7) bounds each retained
depth by D_B(K_j)/M_{T,j}, whose limit is β. The first inequality
holds member by member after canonical lifting. Since

    β<γ_d/h(U)≤γ_d/h(T),

Φ(T) is a smaller bad canonical minor, a contradiction. Hence T=U.
There is a uniform v>0 such that all sufficiently late fibers in the
minimizing sequence have volume at least v.

This argument does not presume any convergence of fiber shapes or
positions. It uses only finitely many normalized masses and the exact
Minkowski inclusions.

## 6. Normalization and compactness on the chosen fixed lift

The base B is dependence-connected, all masses lie in [v,1], and its
finite anchored representations are fixed. The propagation lemma in
Section 3 of `candidate dbf3b23d25004153`
therefore bounds all fiber diameters uniformly after normalizing one
anchor by a determinant-one linear continuous map. A common continuous
translation can be included in this normalization. All these maps
preserve B, compatibility, total mass, and depth.

Let c_{j,u} be the fiber centroids after that step. The finite
representation matrix argument gives a uniform distance bound from
the centroid array to L(B)⊗R^d: each representation row has error at
most the common diameter, because the centroid of the target and the
convex combination of source centroids both belong to the target.
Project the centroid array orthogonally to this space.

By (5), the projected array is the restriction of a vector-valued
ordinary affine function G_j on aff(B). Thus the map

    (b,x)↦(b,x−G_j(b))                                   (10)

is an ambient affine shear. In contrast to arbitrary fiber-dependent
translations, it preserves all ambient halfspaces and their depths.
After (10), all centroids and all fibers are in one fixed ball.

Blaschke compactness, or the compactness of closed convex subsets of a
fixed compact ball, gives a simultaneous Hausdorff-convergent
subsequence K_{j,u}→K_{∞,u}. Compatibility survives by approximating
each chosen source point while keeping the same convex coefficients.
Volumes converge, including at degenerate convex limits. Here every
limiting fiber volume is at least v>0, and their total is one. Hence
the limit is an actual positive family on the same fixed base B.

## 7. Continuity of the maximum depth

The indicators of bounded convex sets converge in L1 under Hausdorff
convergence. At a full-dimensional limit, interior and exterior points
stabilize off its null boundary; at a lower-dimensional limit, the
volumes tend to zero. Summing the finitely many fiber errors gives
total variation convergence of the mixed measures.

Moving a candidate x to x' in one fixed base fiber changes any
halfspace with unit continuous normal by a threshold of at most
|x−x'|. If every fiber is in R B_d, the intervening slab in each fiber
has volume at most κ_{d−1}R^(d−1)|x−x'|. The finite sum gives a
uniform Lipschitz bound for the depth function within each fiber.
Pure base-direction halfspaces do not change under this movement.
Taking the infimum preserves this bound. Total variation controls the
depth change for a fixed candidate by the total variation error.

To pass maxima, take maximizing candidates and a converging subsequence
with fixed base index. Hausdorff convergence puts the limit candidate
in the corresponding limit fiber; the preceding bounds give the
upper-limit inequality. Conversely approximate a limit maximizer in
that fixed original fiber to obtain the lower-limit inequality. Thus

    D_B(K_j)→D_B(K_∞).

This argument retains closed halfspaces with whole fibers on their
boundaries and arbitrary coupling of base and continuous normals.

## 8. Attained-counterexample theorem

Combining the preceding sections proves:

**Theorem.** If a fixed finite base P admits an actual positive fiber
family violating γ_d/h(P), then some canonical lifted closed minor
B=Φ(U) has all the following properties:

1. h(B)=h(U)≤h(P), and U is dependence-connected.
2. Every representation-preserving scalar function on B is affine.
3. The infimum b_d(B)<γ_d/h(B) is attained by an actual family whose
   every fiber has positive d-volume.
4. A normalized minimizing sequence for that infimum has a subsequence
   compact modulo ordinary affine continuous maps and shears on B.

The affine dimension of B is at most h(B)−1. Indeed its affine
dimension is dim L(U)−1, and any r-dimensional finite set has Helly
number at least r+1: use the facets of an r-simplex with vertices in
the set as a minimal infeasible family.

This theorem transfers a strict counterexample to an attained one. It
does not supply an estimate at the attained minimum. Even for an
initial lattice base, the lifted base is treated with its exact finite
Helly number; no claim identifies it with a full mixed-integer lattice
in its possibly larger affine dimension.

## 9. A separate attained minimum with finitely many shared planes

Such a base B also admits a strict bad family whose ambient convex
hull is a polytope. Here is an approximation proof that keeps every
specified fiber. Begin with any strict bad family K_b on B. For each
ε>0 and each b choose a finite ε-net of K_b consisting of points in
K_b, and let A_{ε,b} be its convex hull. Then
A_{ε,b}⊂K_b and their Hausdorff distance is at most ε. Set

    C_ε=conv ⋃_{b∈B} ({b}×A_{ε,b}).

Let K_{ε,b} be the actual b-fiber of C_ε. Compatibility of the original
family gives

    A_{ε,b}⊂K_{ε,b}⊂K_b.

Thus the actual fibers converge individually in Hausdorff distance.
For sufficiently small ε they all have positive d-volume. The body
C_ε has interior in aff(B)×R^d, because B affinely spans its base and
each fiber is full-dimensional. Section 7 gives convergence of their
maximum depths, so a fixed strict violation persists for small ε.
The body C_ε is a polytope and has finitely many facets. A facet
inequality with zero continuous normal depends only on b and is valid
at every specified base point; it imposes no restriction within any
specified fiber and may be dropped. Thus, for some finite N, this
strict bad family has a shared representation

    K_b={x∈R^d: n_f·x+a_f·b≤c_f, 1≤f≤N},
    n_f∈R^d\{0}.                                       (11)

Let R_N(B) be the class of all positive actual families admitting
(11). Repeated or redundant inequalities are allowed. The complexity
bound is on this shared representation, not on the facets of the
canonical hull conv(S). These two bounds need not coincide.

Minimize depth in R_N(B), and denote that infimum by β_N. Then
β_N<γ_d/h(B). The preceding minimality arguments still exclude both
vanishing fiber masses and dependence decompositions, because either
would produce a smaller bad canonical minor in the unrestricted class.
For the minimizing sequence in this class, replace β by β_N in the
mass-discard argument; the same strict inequalities apply. Sections
6–7 consequently give normalized, all-positive Hausdorff limits with
convergent maximum depths. Ordinary continuous linear maps and affine
shears preserve the number N in (11).

For completeness, the shared-representation closure argument from
`candidate d485228e666ca27b` is reproduced here in this more
general finite-base setting. Normalize each n_{f,j} to unit length,
rescaling its entire inequality, and pass to a subsequence with
n_{f,j}→n_f. For each f and b also pass to limits of

    t_{f,j}(b)=c_{f,j}−a_{f,j}·b

in the extended real line. A limit of −∞ is impossible: every
approximating fiber is nonempty and uniformly bounded, so every
threshold is bounded below by minus that common radius. Limits are
therefore finite or +∞.

At any fixed b the finite limiting inequalities represent K_{∞,b}
globally in R^d. One inclusion follows by approximating points of that
fiber. For the other, take an arbitrary point y satisfying the finite
inequalities and a point q with a ball about q contained in K_{∞,b}.
A smaller fixed ball is contained in all late K_{j,b}; thus q satisfies
every finite limiting inequality with a uniform positive margin.
For 0<s<1, the point (1−s)y+s q satisfies each finite inequality
strictly, and every divergent threshold eventually exceeds its fixed
continuous evaluation. Hence this point belongs to K_{j,b} for all
large j. Pass to the Hausdorff limit and then to s↓0. This proves
membership of y in K_{∞,b} and shows that the finite limiting system
is already bounded.

For each fixed f, the finite limits on the set F of base indices are
the restriction of one affine function on B. Indeed, the image E of
the finite affine evaluation map is a linear subspace of R^B, and its
restriction E_F is closed. Choose a linear right inverse for E→E_F.
Correct the approximating evaluation vectors by the right inverse of
their error on F. This correction tends to zero, makes their values
on F exactly equal to the finite limits, and leaves their other
entries tending to +∞. Choose one sufficiently late corrected vector
so that those other entries exceed all relevant support values of the
bounded limiting fibers. The corrected vector is the evaluation of
one actual affine threshold on B.

Do this for each of the N inequalities. At each base point, the
resulting finite thresholds agree exactly with all finite limiting
ones; all former +∞ restrictions are redundant there. Thus (11)
represents every limiting fiber exactly, with N nonzero continuous
normals. This proves closure of R_N(B) at these positive limits.

It follows that β_N is attained by an all-positive family in R_N(B).
This is a polytopal family and still strictly violates γ_d/h(B).
This attained minimum is separate from the unrestricted attained
minimum β in Sections 4–8; no equality β_N=β is asserted.

Finally, arbitrary sufficiently small changes of all coefficients in
(11) remain legitimate local competitors in R_N(B). Positive
interior balls survive small perturbations at the finitely many base
points. Boundedness survives too: the common continuous normals of
a bounded nonempty system have recession cone {0}, equivalently
min_{|u|=1} max_f n_f·u>0. This positive margin persists under small
normal changes. The changed shared inequalities automatically
preserve (1), by taking their convex combinations. Normalize total
mass afterwards by a common continuous dilation if desired.

Thus the shared-plane variational mechanism has an attained,
all-positive, finite-complexity extremal setting after this auxiliary
reduction. Its missing numerical estimate is not supplied here.
